segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those who are not strong, and not to please ourselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Each of us should please our neighbor for what is good, to build them up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even Christ did not please himself, but as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whatever was written beforehand was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another, in accordance with Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that together, with one voice, you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you, to the glory of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I say that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised for the sake of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Therefore I will give thanks to you among the Gentiles, and sing praise to your name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again it says:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again Isaiah says:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The root of Jesse will come, the one who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I myself am convinced about you, my brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able also to admonish one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But on some points I have written to you rather boldly, by way of reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving the good news of God as a priest, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, made holy by the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I have my boast in Christ Jesus in what concerns God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fully proclaimed the good news of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and so making it my ambition to proclaim the good news not where Christ has already been named, so that I would not build on someone else’s foundation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is also why I have so often been hindered from coming to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now I no longer have room to work in these regions, and for many years I have longed to come to you

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whenever I travel to Spain. For I hope to see you as I pass through and to be sent on my way there by you, once I have first enjoyed your company for a while.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now I am going to Jerusalem in service to the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to share something with the poor among the holy ones in Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were pleased to do so, and indeed they are in debt to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when I have completed this and have set the seal on this fruit for them, I will set out for Spain by way of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of Christ’s blessing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urge you, brothers and sisters, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to struggle alongside me in your prayers to God on my behalf,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that I may be rescued from the disobedient in Judea and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the holy ones,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and find rest in your company.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

notes.phrase: and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy
notes.note: The Greek of verses 8–9 is compressed and its grammar is disputed. The rendering takes the Gentiles’ glorifying God as a second purpose of Christ’s becoming a servant of the circumcised, which is the majority view. Others read it as a second statement dependent on “I say”: that the Gentiles, for their part, glorify God for mercy.

The Greek word is the ordinary word for “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. It is the same word in each of the quotations in verses 9–12, where English versions of the Old Testament often have “nations.” Paul strings these passages together because each contains it.

Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 from the Greek version, which differs from the Hebrew, where the root of Jesse “stands as a signal for the peoples.” The verb for “rises” is also a common word for rising from the dead, and many interpreters think Paul heard that overtone here, though the quotation does not require it.

The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it now sounds like a religious term or the name of a book. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

Paul describes his mission in the language of temple worship: the words behind “minister,” “serving as a priest,” and “offering” were all used of sacrificial service. Most interpreters take the offering to be the Gentiles themselves, presented to God through Paul’s work. The Greek could also mean an offering that the Gentiles bring.

The Greek verb is built directly on the word for “holy,” the same word used in “Holy Spirit” in this phrase, and “made holy” keeps that link audible. “Sanctified” is the traditional rendering and means the same thing; the choice is one of clarity, not of meaning.

The manuscripts divide three ways here: “the Spirit,” “the Spirit of God,” and “the Holy Spirit.” The Greek text followed prints the shortest reading, on the view that the longer forms are scribal expansions. Many translations follow “the Spirit of God.” The sense is not affected.

notes.traditional: whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you
notes.note: In the Greek, Paul’s sentence in verses 23–24 breaks off and never reaches its main verb; the translation completes it as smoothly as English allows. Later manuscripts mend the break by adding “I will come to you” after “Spain,” which is why those words appear in the King James Version.

This verb regularly meant more than saying goodbye: it was used of equipping travelers with provisions, money, or companions for the next stage of a journey. Paul is signaling that he hopes the believers in Rome will support his mission to Spain.

The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. “Saints,” the traditional rendering, now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other translations use “God’s people” or “the Lord’s people.”

The noun is the one usually translated “fellowship”; here it names a concrete act of sharing, the money Paul collected from his largely Gentile churches for poor believers in Jerusalem. Most translations say “make a contribution.” “Share” is used so that the link with the related verb in verse 27, “have shared in,” stays visible.

notes.phrase: set the seal on this fruit
notes.note: The exact image is uncertain. Goods were sealed to guarantee that they arrived intact, so the phrase most likely means delivering the collection safely and formally into the hands of the Jerusalem believers, and many translations simply say “delivered.” “Fruit” is the collection, perhaps seen as the produce of the mission among the Gentiles.

The verb’s ordinary meaning is to disobey or refuse to comply, and it stands in contrast to the “obedience” of the Gentiles in verse 18. Many translations have “unbelievers,” since the disobedience in view is refusal of the good news; others have “the disobedient.” Paul means those in Judea who reject the message about Jesus.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs in every letter, and translators divide between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so one policy is needed.
The noun and its verb range over encouragement, comfort, exhortation and appeal across the New Testament, and inconsistent English hides the links between passages.
It is rendered variously as patience, endurance, perseverance or steadfastness, and it recurs in Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation.
Translations split between “disobey” and “not believe” in John, Acts, Romans, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and the choice affects how unbelief is characterized.

This word group (with λειτουργέω and λειτουργία) carries public-service and priestly overtones and must be kept distinct from διάκονος and its relatives, which the register renders “servant” and “service.”

warnings: Verse 13: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
